As of 230 AM EST Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry weather continues into the middle of this week 
with above average temperatures.

Surface analysis shows the area of high pressure still centered over 
our area this morning. This has allowed to winds to fall calm and 
skies to become mostly clear overnight. Guidance is rather 
persistent with more widespread fog developing over the next 
few hours, likely becoming dense in places. Higher confidence 
for fog is east of I-95, so please be on the look out for 
reduced visibilities during the morning commute. Any fog will 
quickly disperse after ~8-9am giving way to mostly clear skies. 
High temperatures today are forecast to be 10-12 degrees warmer 
than yesterday as upper level ridging builds in, with most 
everyone warming up in the low to mid 70s. The warmest 
temperatures will be across SE VA and NE NC where some upper 70s
are possible. More fog is possible Tuesday night, though it 
doesn't look quite as widespread for now. Lows will be warmer 
than this morning as we bottom out in the upper 40s west of 
I-95 and lower to mid 50s to the east. The area of high 
pressure will slide further offshore on Wednesday ahead of the 
approaching weather system from the west. High temperatures will
warm a few additional degrees as the flow aloft becomes more 
southwesterly. Mid to upper 70s are forecast for most of the 
area, though can't rule out an 80 degree reading across 
interior NE NC. Thicker cloud cover will move in later 
Wednesday, keeping low temperatures rather mild around 60 
degrees. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Rain chances increase Thursday night into Friday. 
Locally heavy rainfall is possible, although some uncertainty 
remains regarding rainfall amounts and placement.

Models continue to come in slightly better agreement with the 
evolution of the low pressure system to our west for mid-week and 
beyond. By Wednesday, the closed low will be centered over MN/WI, 
with its associated cold front extending down along the Mississippi 
River Valley. The low then looks to open into a trough as it shifts 
across the Great Lakes on Thursday. The cold front will move into 
the state during the day, as our winds turn southerly and 
dewpoints jump into the mid 60s. Rain chances for the daytime
hours of Thursday have substantially declined. Can't totally 
rule out a stray shower, but the GFS and NAM (who's last day of 
existence is today...thanks for everything, NAM) keep us mostly 
dry during the daylight hours. 

The focus of the rain chances has certainly shifted to Friday 
on most guidance as the cold front potentially lingers over the
area. Current model runs show a line of rainfall developing 
across the area Thursday night and becoming locally heavy in 
spots Friday morning/early afternoon. Still hesitant to place 
too much confidence in these local QPF maxes due to model
differences remaining. However, it is worth noting that both 
the GFS and ECMWF are showing localized maximums of over 2 
inches. But again, uncertainties persist regarding the exact 
placement and magnitude of the heavier precipitation, especially
given the potentially convective nature of the rainfall. With 
that being said, a few thunderstorms will be possible Thursday 
night into Friday, though the degree of instability looks to be 
rather low. Low pressure will become better organized across 
Quebec Friday night into Saturday, abruptly sending the cold 
front offshore. This will bring an end to any rain chances for 
the weekend. 

High temperatures will be well above normal on Thursday ahead 
of the front with mid to upper 70s forecast, and perhaps even 
80 degrees across interior NE NC. Only modest cooling is 
expected behind the front, with low to mid 70s on Friday and 
lower 70s on Saturday. Widespread low to mid 60s (which is 
normal for this time of year) look to make a return to start the
new week.
